dmm-2016-team-01.title: Colouring bound and a packing
dmm-2016-team-01.body:
Each T-tetromino has area $4$, so at most $\lfloor36/4\rfloor=9$ fit. Colour the board like a chessboard: $18$ white squares. Every T covers either $1$ or $3$ white squares (odd), so $9$ pieces would cover an odd number of white squares, which is impossible as $9$ pieces cover $36$ squares $=18$ white. Hence at most $8$.

Eight fit (letters mark the pieces, `.` are empty):
```
AAABBB
CAD.BE
CCDDEE
CFDGHE
FFGGHH
.F.GH.
```

**Answer: 8**

dmm-2016-team-02.title: Cyclic quadrilateral
dmm-2016-team-02.body:
$\angle BEC=\angle BDC=90^\circ$, so $D,E$ lie on the circle with diameter $BC$. In the right triangle $ABE$, $\angle ABE=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ$, so the inscribed angle $\angle DBE=60^\circ$ subtends the chord $DE$. Hence $DE=BC\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2BC$ and $\frac{DE}{BC}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}2$**

dmm-2016-team-03.title: Solve the system
dmm-2016-team-03.body:
Replacing $x$ by $1-x$: $2f(1-x)+f(x)=(1-x)^2$. Multiply the original equation by $2$ and subtract: $3f(x)=2x^2-(1-x)^2=x^2+2x-1$, so $f(x)=\frac{x^2+2x-1}3$ (check: $2f(x)+f(1-x)=\frac{2x^2+4x-2+x^2-4x+2}3=x^2$). The sum of squares of the coefficients is $\frac{1+4+1}9=\frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

dmm-2016-team-04.title: Modular obstructions
dmm-2016-team-04.body:
Let $k=n-a_n^2=15m^2-a_n^2\ge0$, so $a_n^2=15m^2-k$. Squares are $0,1$ mod $3$ and $0,1,4$ mod $5$, and $15m^2\equiv0$ modulo $3$ and $5$, so $-k\equiv0,1\pmod3$ and $-k\equiv0,1,4\pmod5$, i.e. $k\equiv0,2\pmod3$ and $k\equiv0,1,4\pmod5$. Checking $k=0,\dots,5$: $k=0$ would make $15m^2$ a square (impossible); $k=1,4$ fail mod $3$; $k=2,3$ fail mod $5$; $k=5$ gives $a_n^2=15m^2-5\equiv-m^2-1\equiv2,3\pmod4$, impossible. So $k\ge6$, and $k=6$ occurs: $m=7$, $n=735$, $a_n=27$ ($27^2=729$, $28^2=784>735$), $n-a_n^2=6$.

**Answer: 6**

dmm-2016-team-05.title: Conjugate sum
dmm-2016-team-05.body:
$S_n=(2+\sqrt5)^n+(2-\sqrt5)^n$ is an integer with $S_0=2,S_1=4$ and $S_n=4S_{n-1}+S_{n-2}$. Since $0<(\sqrt5-2)^{2016}<1$, $\lfloor(\sqrt5+2)^{2016}\rfloor=S_{2016}-1$. Modulo $100$ the sequence $S_n$ is periodic with period $20$ (it returns to $2,4$), so $S_{2016}\equiv S_{16}\pmod{100}$. Computing, $S_{16}\equiv22\pmod{100}$. Hence the last two digits are $22-1=21$.

**Answer: 21**

dmm-2016-team-07.title: Character sum
dmm-2016-team-07.body:
Let $\chi(d)=1$ if $d\equiv1$, $-1$ if $d\equiv3\pmod 4$ and $0$ for even $d$. Then $D_1-D_3=\sum_{d\mid N}\chi(d)=\prod_{p^e\parallel N}(1+\chi(p)+\dots+\chi(p)^e)$ since $\chi$ is multiplicative. The factor is $1$ for $p=2$, $e+1$ for $p\equiv1\pmod4$, and for $p\equiv3\pmod4$ it is $1$ if $e$ is even and $0$ if $e$ is odd. So we need every prime $\equiv3\pmod4$ (in particular $3$ and $7$) to have an even exponent and the primes $\equiv1\pmod4$ to satisfy $\prod(e_p+1)=6$, e.g. $5^5$ or $5^2\cdot13$. Take $N=5^5\cdot3^2\cdot7^2=1378125$, a multiple of $21$.

**Answer (one example): $5^5\cdot3^2\cdot7^2$**

dmm-2016-team-08.title: Count lattice points
dmm-2016-team-08.body:
$\lfloor i^{3/2}\rfloor$ is the number of lattice points $(i,y)$ with $1\le y\le i^{3/2}$, i.e. on or below the curve $y=x^{3/2}$ at $x=i$. Since $x=y^{2/3}$ is the inverse function, $\lfloor j^{2/3}\rfloor$ is the number of lattice points $(x,j)$ with $1\le x\le j^{2/3}$, i.e. on or to the left of the curve at height $j$. As $100^{3/2}=1000$, the two sums together count every lattice point of the rectangle $[1,100]\times[1,1000]$ (that is $100\cdot1000$ points), and the points lying exactly on the curve are counted twice: $x^{3/2}$ is an integer iff $x$ is a perfect square, giving $10$ points. The total is $100000+10=100010$.

**Answer: 100010**

dmm-2016-team-09.title: Inclusion-exclusion
dmm-2016-team-09.body:
For each element, the pair (in $A$?, in $B$?) is one of $4$ equally likely options; $A\subseteq B$ excludes only "in $A$ not in $B$", so $P(A\subseteq B)=\left(\frac34\right)^{10}$, and likewise $P(B\subseteq A)$. Both happen iff $A=B$, which has probability $\left(\frac12\right)^{10}$. So the probability is $2\left(\frac34\right)^{10}-\left(\frac12\right)^{10}=\frac{2\cdot3^{10}-2^{10}}{4^{10}}=\frac{58537}{524288}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\cdot3^{10}-2^{10}}{4^{10}}$**

dmm-2016-team-10.title: Every person is on exactly 5 teams
dmm-2016-team-10.body:
*No person is on 6 teams.* Suppose $a$ is on teams $B_1,\dots,B_6$; they pairwise share only $a$. Take $b\in B_1$, $b'\in B_2$ (both $\ne a$). By (2) some team $C$ contains $b$ and $b'$. Then $a\notin C$ (otherwise $C\cap B_1\supseteq\{a,b\}$ would have two members, and $C\ne B_1$ since $b'\notin B_1$). $C$ meets each of $B_3,\dots,B_6$ in exactly one person; these four people are distinct (the $B_i$ share only $a$) and differ from $b,b'$. So $C$ has at least $2+4=6$ members, a contradiction.

*No person is on at most $4$ teams.* Let $a$ be on teams $B_1,\dots,B_t$ with $t\le4$. By (2) every person shares a team with $a$, so everyone lies in some $B_i$. A team $C$ not containing $a$ meets each $B_i$ in exactly one person, and all its members lie in $\bigcup B_i$, so $|C|=t\le4<5$: contradiction. So every team contains $a$; but then two teams share only $a$ and, for $b,b'$ in different teams, no team contains both: contradiction (there are $\ge2$ teams).

So every person is on exactly $5$ teams. Fix a team $T_0$; each of the other teams meets it in exactly one of its $5$ members and each member lies on $4$ other teams. So there are $1+5\cdot4=21$ teams (and $m=21$: this is the projective plane of order $4$).

**Answer: 21**
